slides.narration_text: Let's turn to the chain. Alignment is not a stack of pretty boxes, and it is not a hope you write at the top of a page. It is one metal chain with five links still fastened: Objective, Evidence, Practice, Feedback, and Access. If a link opens, later choices cannot carry the load. For each focal objective, name acceptable evidence first, before you fall in love with an activity. Then name the practice that would produce that evidence. Then say how feedback will be used, not merely collected. Then keep the fifth link: what your modality and access choices do to who can actually perform. Engagement, completion, confidence, and satisfaction are not automatically evidence of learning. They can be useful signals. They are not the target. Practice the target performance before you judge it. Two focal objectives. Reuse the same IDs across Panels 2 through 5 so the file does not grow a second secret curriculum. A plan that stops at feedback is not yet aligned. The last link is still fastened for a reason. Hold the chain in your hand when you open Panel 3.

slides.visual_description: Caption: Modality is a design tradeoff because the room you choose changes what learners can actually do. Labels: Modality Is a Design Tradeoff; online; live; classroom. Subject: one lesson forking into three paths, with a gap on one path and a parallel walkway beside it. Not a four-cell tool grid.
slides.narration_text: In this section we treat modality as what it is. The Canvas discussion is titled Modality Is a Design Tradeoff. Use that title when you post. A learning goal sits at the fork. One path is online. One is live. One is the classroom. None of those rooms is automatically better, cheaper, or more rigorous. Each one trades something: time, presence, the kind of practice you can see, and who can get in. If the path you wanted is blocked, you still owe the objective. You do not owe the original room. That dashed walkway is the workaround: an equivalent path with an instructional reason, not a shrug and not a tool you happened to have licensed. On Panel 4, every phase is Asynchronous or Live, and you can say why in a sentence a colleague would accept. Name a likely barrier. Name a credible equivalent. Post from the tradeoff, not from a preference for cameras or for quiet. Efficiency versus evidence should feel like a design choice you can defend when someone asks who got left off the path.

They are three levers on the same blueprint. Piskurich helps you diagnose the need, name the outcome, and reserve shared time for application instead of covering. Gagné, in the Kurt 2021 reading, helps you design the experience as a sequence of events matched to what is actually being learned, not a template you fill because it has nine boxes. UDL, CAST 2.2 and Davis and colleagues, asks you to remove barriers so more learners can represent, engage, and express without waiting for a retrofit. Use them at a decision, not as a chapter you have to cover. Name a design basis on the Blueprint where a choice actually changed. Do not survey pages. Piskurich chapters 10 and 11, Gagné's events, and UDL 2.2 earn their keep when they move a phase, an access path, or a piece of evidence.
